newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal faces controversial abortion vote.
newsitem.headline: Portugal faces controversial abortion vote.

text.p: In an emotion-charged atmosphere, Portugal's parliament votes on Thursday on calls to liberalise one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws, but the signs are that the reformers will be defeated.

Thirteen years after Roman Catholic Portugal allowed abortion under certain circumstances, a bid by left-wingers to sweep away many of the limits seemed likely to fail by a handful of votes, political analysts said.

"Liberalisation set to fail," ran a headline in O Public newspaper on Thursday after the paper did a survey of the relative strengths in parliament, where the major parties are imposing no party line on their representatives.
Portugal allows abortion with no time limit in cases where the mother's life is in danger and in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy where her health, physical or psychological, is at serious risk.

But critics say that the latter is interpreted so restrictively that the number of legal abortions carried out in this country of 10 million -- just 275 in 1995 -- is no more than a drop in the ocean compared with the number of illegal terminations.
The result is that bungled illegal abortions are one of the main causes of maternal mortality in the country, they say.

Two draft bills being presented on Thursday by the small Portuguese Communist Party and the Young Socialists, the youth wing of the ruling party, would sweep away all limits to abortion in the first 12 weeks, making it effectively on demand.
They would also lengthen the period when abortion can be carried out in the case of under-age rape to 16 weeks, from the current 12, and extend that for deformed foetuses to 24 from 16 weeks.
A third bill, proposed by a Socialist deputy, which would merely extend the period to 24 weeks in the case of problems with the foetus appeared likely to pass, political sources said.

Most Socialists back the changes, but with some known defections and the party four seats short of a majority in the 230-seat parliament, the outcome could depend on the number of abstentions on both sides.

The main opposition Social Democrats are predominantly opposed to the bills, while the votes of the Communists and the right-wing Popular Party, which is fiercely anti-abortion, will cancel each other out.
Campaigning ahead of the vote, which is not expected until very late on Thursday, has been fierce with both sides accusing the other of trickery and emotional blackmail.

An image used by the Catholic, anti-abortion 'Together for Life' group of a supposedly 12-week-old foetus, with the caption "Would you kill this child", turned out to be that of a foetus several weeks older.
Whatever the outcome of the debate, the vote may not be the final word on the issue.
The ruling Socialists have promised that they will call a national referendum if the Communist and Young Socialist motions pass in parliament.
